description: Livermorium Tech is a student-led team from SMAN 116 Jakarta, driven by a shared passion for space exploration, aerospace, and engineering. We aim to combine scientific curiosity, technical creativity, and engineering problem-solving to explore innovative solutions to real-world challenges, particularly those related to space and future exploration.
summary:
ASTRA (Astronaut Sensing, Tracking & Radiation Analysis) is a proposed astronaut health-monitoring system designed to help monitor radiation exposure during space missions. Developed by Livermorium Tech from SMAN 116 Jakarta, ASTRA addresses the risks of space radiation, including Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) and Solar Particle Events (SPEs), which can affect astronaut health.

Our project combines a proposed wearable sensor system with an interactive software dashboard. The wearable concept uses distributed sensor modules attached to or integrated into an astronaut's clothing to collect radiation-related measurements. The software then presents this information through a dashboard displaying sensor readings, radiation conditions, and estimated exposure.

One of ASTRA's main features is an anatomical visualization that uses a simplified 3D human-body model to illustrate how radiation exposure could affect different areas of the body. This makes complex radiation data easier to understand and helps astronauts and mission teams review potential risks.

ASTRA is important because monitoring radiation exposure is essential for safer, long-duration space missions. Our current demonstration uses illustrative data and a proposed hardware design, with future development focused on testing real sensors and improving the accuracy of its exposure models.
details:
ASTRA (Astronaut Sensing, Tracking & Radiation Analysis) is a proposed system designed to help monitor radiation exposure and support astronaut safety during space missions. It combines a wearable sensor concept with an interactive software dashboard to make radiation information easier to understand and review.

The proposed wearable system uses small sensor modules placed within or attached to an astronaut's clothing. These modules are intended to collect radiation-related measurements. The software dashboard then displays this information through sensor readings, radiation levels, and an anatomical visualization. One of ASTRA's main features is a simplified 3D human-body model that illustrates how radiation exposure could affect different areas of the body. This gives users a more visual understanding of radiation risks instead of relying only on numbers and charts.

The main benefit of ASTRA is that it could help astronauts and mission teams become more aware of radiation exposure and make better decisions during missions. Our intended impact is to support safer long-duration space exploration, especially missions that travel beyond Earth's natural protection from space radiation.

We developed our interactive prototype using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The software includes a mission overview, anatomical model, sensor telemetry, and data and methods sections. We also designed a concept for the wearable hardware. At this stage, the hardware is still a proposed design, and the software demonstration uses illustrative data rather than measurements from real sensors.

What makes ASTRA creative is its combination of wearable monitoring and visual data presentation. Instead of simply reporting radiation levels, it attempts to connect the information to a model of the human body. During development, our team considered astronaut comfort, sensor placement, ease of use, data clarity, and the challenges of maintaining equipment in space. We also considered the need for removable sensor modules and washable clothing components.

ASTRA is our first step toward exploring how technology and software could work together to improve astronaut health monitoring and make future space missions safer.
